title: Model Results
text:
The SEA Provinces Study examines dengue incidence rate prediction at the admin-1 (province) level across 10 Southeast Asian countries. The study uses a Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network (STGNN) to model the temporal dynamics of dengue incidence while leveraging spatial relationships between provinces. We experiment with a number of message passing configurations to empirically examine both how well and through what mechanism does a model manage to capture whether dengue risk ebbs and flows display interprovincial effects.
In our final risk index for Southeast Asia, we use the same learned temporal and spatial patterns to generate a risk index for each province, which can be used to inform public health interventions and resource allocation.
Notes: The gap of incomplete incidence data between 2019 and 2026 is due to a coverage imbalance. To counter act this, the 2011-2018 model will continue to learn and predict between 2019 and 2026, but the predictions will be unvalidated. Thus, interpretation of the latest monthly risk must be done with caution, and the model’s predictions should be used as a guide rather than a definitive measure of risk.

title: Model Results
text:
Architecture
The model is a Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Network with GRU (STGATGRU):

Input normalisation: log1p target transform, then standard-scaled (mean/std from training data); calendar seasonality is supplied as sin/cos month-of-year features rather than removed from the target (see the experiment descriptions below)
GAT layer 1: Spatial message passing over the admin-1 adjacency graph
MLP: Node-wise feature transformation
GAT layer 2: Second spatial aggregation pass
GRU: Temporal sequence modelling over a sliding window (window length is a per-experiment hyperparameter — see each experiment’s Hyperparameters table below)
Linear head: Single-step incidence rate prediction (inverse-transformed at output)

Missing admin-1 nodes (no reported incidence) receive a learnable missing embedding rather than zeroed features, and the GRU hidden state is carried over without update for those nodes. Loss masking excludes missing targets from the gradient.

title: Model Results
text:
Bias Correction Note
When the climate-only model runs on current data (post-2018), a climate delta correction is applied before features are passed to the model. The delta is observational: for each variable and calendar month, the 2019–2026 mean of the same ERA5-Land / CHIRPS / MODIS products minus the 2011–2018 training-period mean. This shifts current observations back into the model’s training feature distribution, so the risk index reflects how unusual a month is for today’s climate rather than the long-term shift itself. See site/scripts/apply_climate_delta.py for implementation.

title: Model Results
text:
Experiment Results
We show one experiment here: cyclical_seasonal. It predicts log incidence rate (log IR) from lagged IR plus climate and land-use covariates, encodes calendar month with the sin/cos cyclical encoding (rather than subtracting a fixed per-month training baseline — see the Bias Correction Note above for why that matters beyond the training window), and gives missing admin-1 nodes a learned trainable embedding rather than zeroed-out features (see Architecture above). Its hyperparameters are also the ones the climate-only model behind the live risk map is trained with.
The results below come from its config/training run under machine-learning-module/results/STGNN/: metrics, hyperparameters, training curves, and available plots.

title: Model Results
text:
As dengue epidemics in Taiwan are results of imported cases from circulating dengue transmission in Southeast Asia, we capitalise on our Southeast Asian interprovincial risk state model to generate “exporter” regions and “importer” regions into our Taiwanese BSA model. A BSA is the smallest unit of census data the Taiwanese Government keeps track of.
The model would jointly consider international mobility, local mobility, BSA environment suitability, and BSA population demographic to predict elevated risk.

title: Spatiotemporal Dengue Risk Prediction in Southeast Asia and Taiwan

title: Spatiotemporal Dengue Risk Prediction in Southeast Asia and Taiwan
text:
Study Overview
This project combines two complementary prediction models targeting different geographic scales and use cases:


Arm 1 — Southeast Asia Provinces
A spatiotemporally-aware deep learning model (ST-GAT + GRU) trained on 162 admin-1 provinces across 10 SEA countries (2011–2018). It captures international dengue risk dynamics using province-level historical infection data, monthly climatological data (ERA5-Land, VIIRS, CHIRPS v3 for the live climate model; MODIS and CHIRPS v2 in the study), and Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. Inference runs monthly; the climate-only risk map is bias-corrected for the observed post-2018 climate shift.
View SEA Provinces Results →


Arm 2 — Taiwan Basic Statistics Area (BSA)
A Taiwan-specific counterpart operating at the finer granularity of the Basic Statistics Area (BSA) — the smallest census unit tracked by the Taiwanese government. It jointly considers international mobility (using SEA risk states from Arm 1 as exporter signals), local mobility, BSA-level environmental suitability, and population demographics to predict elevated local dengue risk.
View Taiwan BSA Results →

title: Spatiotemporal Dengue Risk Prediction in Southeast Asia and Taiwan
text:
About
Dengue fever’s transmission dynamics in Southeast Asia relies on human and vector mobility, displaying a high degree of non-linearity and unpredictability. Moreover, as dengue outbreaks in Taiwan are attributed to imported cases from Southeast Asia coinciding with windows of time where weather favors vector reproductability, preventative measures must be taken at the right time in the right places. To address the limits of considering dengue outbreak in isolation which ignores how circulating dengue serotypes confer patterns that may only be explained across multiple countries extended beyond neighboring years, this study creates a two-pronged experimental design that combines: (1) a Southeast Asian spatiotemporally-aware deep learning prediction model that captures international dengue risk dynamics based on province-level historical infection data, near-real-time climatological data, as well as Shared Socioeconomic Pathways data. (2) a Taiwan-only counterpart whose prediction works at a finer granularity, a Basic Statistics Area (BSA), and predicts based on individual case report, clinical diagnosis, demographic data, and environmental data.


SEA Provinces Pipeline

Monthly zonal statistics fetched from Google Earth Engine
Observational climate delta (2019–2026 vs 2011–2018) applied to adjust for post-2018 climate shift
STGNN inference run on adjusted features
Results published automatically via GitHub Actions

Architecture: ST-GAT + GRU (PyTorch Geometric) Training period: 2011–2018 Features: ERA5-Land, MODIS LST, NDVI/EVI, CHIRPS, LULC, WorldPop, SSP population Spatial scope: 162 admin-1 regions across 10 SEA countries Performance (test set): Huber 0.390 · MAE 1.214 · RMSE 2.460 (log IR, 14 held-out months)


Taiwan BSA Pipeline

SEA province risk states ingested as international mobility proxy (from Arm 1)
BSA-level environmental suitability computed from TCCIP climate data
Individual case reports and demographic data from Taiwan Ministry of Health
BSA model inference generates sub-district risk predictions

Architecture: (to be finalised) Training period: (to be determined) Features: MoH case reports, clinical diagnosis, demographics, TCCIP climate, local mobility Spatial scope: Taiwan Basic Statistics Areas (BSAs) Performance: (pending model training)




Interpretation note: SEA predictions are expressed as a relative risk index (predicted log IR normalised to the 2011–2018 baseline), not absolute case counts. This accounts for structural model uncertainty arising from the 8-year gap between training data and current conditions.

title: Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
text: Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) are a set of five global scenarios describing plausible futures for societal development through 2100 (SSP1–SSP5). They were developed by the climate research community alongside the IPCC AR6 process and are widely used to contextualise climate impact projections. In this study:
